strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant limitation of Reservoir Computing: sequential processing and memory footprint of dense high-dimensional reservoirs, by porting the diagonal complex linear recurrence and associative-scan parallelization strategy from LRU/SSMs into the RC paradigm.

Provides theoretical grounding: a clean necessary-and-sufficient condition for the Echo State Property under a diagonal complex transition matrix (Theorem 4.1), and a proof that any linear ESN can be represented by an equivalent diagonal complex ParalESN via diagonalization (Proposition 4.2), leading to a universality corollary for the model class.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning memory-capacity tasks, chaotic/real-world forecasting, UEA/UCR classification, and 1-D pixel-level classification (sMNIST/psMNIST), together with a computational complexity analysis (Appendix B) and comparisons against other structured RC variants (SCR, Structured RC) and fully-trainable models (LSTM, Transformer, LRU, Mamba).

Reports concrete and consistent efficiency gains (training time, energy consumption, CO2 emissions) alongside accuracy, and demonstrates scaling to reservoir sizes where traditional dense ESNs run out of memory (Fig. 2), which is a practically meaningful contribution.

Includes hyperparameter sensitivity analysis and critical-difference statistical comparison plots, improving transparency of the empirical claims, and appendices with substantial detail on datasets and experimental protocol that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely an application of existing ideas (LRU's diagonal complex linear recurrence and parallel scan) to the RC setting; the main theoretical argument (Proposition 4.2) is essentially the same diagonalization argument already used to justify LRU, limiting originality.

Accuracy improvements over traditional RC are inconsistent across benchmarks: ParalESN (deep) is sometimes worse than ESN (deep) (e.g., SinMem20, ctXOR10, several ETT forecasting metrics), which somewhat undercuts the claim that the method 'matches' or improves upon traditional RC predictive accuracy uniformly.

Evaluation is restricted to relatively short/small-scale sequence benchmarks (classic RC memory/forecasting tasks, MNIST-scale classification); no evaluation on longer-sequence or larger-scale tasks (e.g., Long Range Arena) that are standard for assessing parallelizable SSM-style architectures and where the claimed logarithmic-time scaling advantage would be most consequential.

Comparisons to fully-trainable baselines (LSTM, Transformer, LRU, Mamba) use fixed, relatively small parameter budgets and limited training epochs (100 with early stopping), raising questions about whether these baselines are fully optimized, which could affect the fairness of the performance/efficiency trade-off claims.

The mixing layer (random convolutional kernel) is a somewhat ad hoc design choice with limited justification beyond a sensitivity sweep; its role in compensating for the loss of cross-unit interaction from the diagonal transition matrix is not rigorously analyzed, and no ablation isolates its individual contribution to overall performance.

No explicit statement about code/artifact release, which combined with the many hyperparameters and per-layer configurations reported (Table 8) creates a moderate reproducibility burden despite the detailed appendix.
